riddle_text: An iron lady stands sentinel over a city of light, her latticed silhouette piercing the sky since a world's fair announced her arrival. Lovers flock to her shadow, artists to her likeness. She was meant to be temporary — and yet here she remains, the most photographed woman in the world.

clues.text: Constructed for an 1889 exposition, this structure was once the tallest man-made object on Earth.
She stands on the Champ de Mars, beside a river that winds through one of Europe's most celebrated capitals.
The city she watches over is famous for its cuisine, fashion, and a certain revolutionary storming of a prison.
This iron tower in Paris, France, is one of the most recognisable structures on Earth.

fun_fact: The Eiffel Tower grows by up to 15cm in summer due to thermal expansion of the iron.

riddle_text: High in the clouds where eagles dare not fly alone, a civilisation carved perfection from the living rock. No mortar holds these stones — only geometry and genius. The Spanish never found it. The jungle swallowed it for centuries. A Yale professor stumbled upon it in 1911 and changed history.

clues.text: This Incan citadel sits at 2,430 metres above sea level, wrapped in cloud forest and mountain mist.
Located in the Cusco Region, it overlooks the Sacred Valley of the Urubamba River.
It is the most visited tourist destination in South America, in a country known for llamas and ancient empires.
This famous Incan ruin in Peru was declared one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

fun_fact: Machu Picchu was built without the use of the wheel, iron tools, or mortar.

riddle_text: Fifty thousand souls once roared within these walls as sand ran red and glory was measured in survival. Emperors sat in judgement while the crowd decided fate with a turn of a thumb. Two thousand years of earthquakes, floods, and plunder have stripped her bones — yet still she stands, defiant and eternal.

clues.text: This amphitheatre was completed in 80 AD under Emperor Titus and could hold up to 80,000 spectators.
It stands near the Roman Forum in a city built on seven hills beside the Tiber River.
The country it sits in is shaped like a boot and is home to more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other nation.
This ancient Roman arena in Rome, Italy, once hosted gladiatorial combat.

fun_fact: The Colosseum could be flooded to stage mock naval battles called naumachiae.

riddle_text: Like sails frozen mid-voyage, her white shells billow above a harbour of sapphire and steel. A Danish architect dreamed her into existence on the back of a lottery ticket — then never saw her completed. She is the sound of a continent finding its voice, a nation's soul expressed in concrete and ceramic.

clues.text: Designed by Jørn Utzon, this building took 14 years to complete and opened in 1973.
It sits on Bennelong Point, jutting into one of the world's most beautiful natural harbours.
The city surrounding it is the largest in a country where kangaroos outnumber people.
This iconic performing arts centre with sail-like roofs sits in Sydney Harbour, Australia.

fun_fact: The Sydney Opera House's roof tiles are self-cleaning — rain washes them automatically.

riddle_text: Rose-red and half as old as time, she hides behind a narrow crack in the desert rock — the Siq, a mile-long canyon that exhales you suddenly into her treasury's face. The Nabataeans carved an entire civilisation from the living cliff. Crusaders, traders, and conquerors searched for her and failed. A fictional archaeologist with a whip found her.

clues.text: This ancient city was the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom and is sometimes called the Rose City for the colour of its sandstone.
It is accessed through a narrow gorge called the Siq, and its most famous structure is Al-Khazneh — the Treasury.
Located in a desert country bordered by Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Syria, known for Bedouin culture and the Dead Sea.
This famous carved rock city in Jordan was used as a filming location for Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade.

fun_fact: Petra was the capital of a civilisation that controlled the incense trade route worth billions in today's money.

riddle_text: The largest religious monument on Earth was built not to the God of Abraham but to Vishnu — then repurposed to Buddha when the wind of faith changed direction. Jungle strangled her for five centuries while empires rose and fell. Her towers, like lotus buds, still pierce the morning mist at the moment of perfect sunrise.

clues.text: Built in the 12th century under King Suryavarman II, this temple complex covers 402 acres — the largest religious monument in the world.
It appears on the national flag of its country and is surrounded by a moat stretching 5km in circumference.
Located near Siem Reap in a Southeast Asian country that endured the devastating Khmer Rouge regime in the 1970s.
This ancient Hindu-Buddhist temple complex in Cambodia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by millions annually.

fun_fact: Angkor Wat was built by an estimated 300,000 workers and 6,000 elephants over 37 years.

riddle_text: A volcano's rage hollowed her heart into a lagoon of impossible blue. White cubic houses teeter on the edge of the caldera like dice stacked by a careless god. Blue domes catch the Aegean light. Some say she is all that remains of Atlantis — a myth, perhaps, but the sunset here does feel like the end of the world.

clues.text: This island's current crescent shape was formed by a catastrophic volcanic eruption around 1600 BC — one of the largest in human history.
Its villages of Oia and Fira are renowned for their whitewashed architecture and panoramic views over an ancient caldera.
Located in the Cyclades island group of a Mediterranean country known as the birthplace of democracy.
This famous Greek island with iconic white and blue buildings is one of the most photographed places in Europe.

fun_fact: Santorini's volcanic eruption may have contributed to the collapse of the Minoan civilisation on Crete.

riddle_text: Pillars of quartzite sandstone rise from the mist like the fingers of a buried god, their peaks draped in cloud and twisted pine. A filmmaker saw them and placed a floating world in the sky above. Bridges span the abyss between them. Glass walkways hug their vertical faces, daring the faint-hearted to look down.

clues.text: This park's unique pillar formations inspired the floating Hallelujah Mountains in the 2009 James Cameron film Avatar.
It was the world's first national forest park when designated in 1982 and features over 3,000 quartzite sandstone pillars.
Located in Hunan Province of the world's most populous country, famous for the Great Wall and the Yangtze River.
These dramatic rock pillar formations in Hunan, China, inspired the landscape in Avatar.

fun_fact: One of Zhangjiajie's pillars was officially renamed Avatar Hallelujah Mountain after the film's release.

riddle_text: At dawn, a hundred silk envelopes fill with fire and rise silently above a landscape that looks like the moon forgot to be barren. Volcanic ash carved by rain and wind over millennia formed spires they call fairy chimneys. Entire civilisations burrowed underground here to escape persecution — their cities descend twelve storeys into the earth.

clues.text: This region's distinctive fairy chimney rock formations were created by the erosion of volcanic ash from ancient eruptions, primarily of Mount Erciyes.
It is famous for underground cities — Derinkuyu and Kaymaklı — which could shelter tens of thousands of people from invaders.
Located in Anatolia, in a country that straddles Europe and Asia and is home to Istanbul and Ankara.
This Turkish region is world-famous for hot air balloon rides over its unique fairy chimney rock formations.

fun_fact: The underground city of Derinkuyu could accommodate 20,000 people and had its own wineries, stables, and churches.

riddle_text: Here grows a tree that bleeds — its sap as red as the name they gave it — Dragon's Blood. Its canopy spreads flat like an opened umbrella, alien and ancient, evolved in isolation for twenty million years. The island it calls home is so remote, so biologically distinct, that scientists named it the Galapagos of the Indian Ocean.

clues.text: This island is home to the Dragon Blood Tree (Dracaena cinnabari), found nowhere else on Earth, with its distinctive umbrella-shaped canopy and crimson resin.
It has been isolated from the mainland for so long that 37% of its plant species are entirely endemic — found nowhere else on Earth.
It lies in the Arabian Sea off the Gulf of Aden and is administered by a country currently experiencing a severe humanitarian crisis.
This remote island in Yemen is famous for its alien-looking Dragon Blood Trees and extraordinary endemic wildlife.

fun_fact: The Dragon Blood Tree's red sap was historically used as a violin varnish, a dye, and a medicine.

riddle_text: Eighteen islands of volcanic rock thrust from the North Atlantic like a raised fist. Sheep outnumber people here three to one — the name itself means Sheep Islands. Grass grows on the rooftops, not as decoration but as ancient tradition. The light here is liquid, the weather changes every four minutes, and the roads end at clifftops above the open ocean.

clues.text: This archipelago has a population of around 55,000 people and approximately 70,000 sheep. It is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
The islands are known for Múlafossur waterfall, the village of Gásadalur, and dramatic sea cliffs. Their capital is Tórshavn, one of the smallest capitals in the world.
Located halfway between Norway and Iceland in the North Atlantic Ocean, with no land bridge to any other country.
These remote Danish autonomous islands in the North Atlantic are known for dramatic cliffs, turf-roofed houses, and vast numbers of sheep.

fun_fact: The Faroe Islands have their own language, Faroese, which is descended from Old Norse and has approximately 70,000 speakers.

riddle_text: The world's largest mirror lies at altitude — ten thousand square kilometres of crystallised time, the dried bed of a prehistoric lake that evaporated and left its bones as salt. When rain falls, it coats the surface in a film of water so perfect it doubles the sky. Flamingos wade at its edges. Cacti-covered islands rise from its white centre.

clues.text: This 10,582 km² salt flat sits at 3,656 metres above sea level and contains more than half the world's known lithium reserves.
After rain, its mirror-flat surface reflects the sky with such perfect fidelity it is used to calibrate the altimeters of Earth observation satellites.
Located in a landlocked South American country that lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884).
This vast white salt flat in Bolivia becomes the world's largest mirror after rainfall.

fun_fact: Salar de Uyuni is so flat that its surface varies by less than one metre across its entire 10,000 km² area.

riddle_text: Two thousand temples rise from a dusty plain beside a great river, their red-brick spires puncturing an orange sky at dusk. Once there were ten thousand — war, earthquake, and the bite of time have reduced their number but not their grandeur. A kingdom that ruled this land for two centuries poured its devotion into the earth itself, brick by brick, prayer by prayer.

clues.text: This ancient city was the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from the 9th to 13th centuries. At its peak, over 10,000 Buddhist temples were built across its plain.
It sits beside the Irrawaddy River and was largely abandoned after Kublai Khan's Mongol forces sacked the kingdom in 1287.
Located in a Southeast Asian country formerly known as Burma, bordered by Thailand, China, Laos, India, and Bangladesh.
This plain of ancient Buddhist temples in Myanmar is one of Asia's most significant archaeological sites.

fun_fact: An earthquake in 2016 damaged hundreds of Bagan's temples, but the Myanmar government controversially restored many with non-historical materials.

riddle_text: In the kingdom of perpetual winter, polar bears outnumber people and the sun either never rises or never sets depending on the season. A seed vault bored into the permafrost here holds backup copies of every crop on Earth — a Noah's Ark for the apocalypse. Carry a rifle outside town; the rule here is not the law of man but the law of the ice.

clues.text: This archipelago hosts the Global Seed Vault, carved into a mountain, containing over 1.3 million seed varieties from almost every country on Earth.
It has approximately 3,500 polar bears — significantly more than its human population — and it is illegal to leave the main settlement without a firearm.
Located in the Arctic Ocean, it is a Norwegian territory and the world's northernmost permanently inhabited settlement — Longyearbyen — is found here.
This Norwegian Arctic archipelago is home to the Global Seed Vault and has more polar bears than people.

fun_fact: It is illegal to die in Longyearbyen — the permafrost prevents bodies from decomposing, so terminally ill residents must be flown to mainland Norway.

riddle_text: A desert of rust and silence — sandstone monoliths rise like cathedrals from a valley of red sand, carved by wind into arches and canyons over millennia. Lawrence rode through here on a camel before the world changed. Mars rovers have tested their cameras here. Bedouins still sleep under stars so dense they seem within reach.

clues.text: This desert valley was used as a filming location for The Martian, Dune, Rogue One, and Lawrence of Arabia due to its resemblance to the Martian surface.
It is known as the Valley of the Moon and contains ancient Nabataean and Thamudic rock inscriptions.
Located in the southernmost part of the same country that contains Petra, near the Red Sea port of Aqaba and the Saudi Arabian border.
This dramatic red desert valley in Jordan was used as a Mars stand-in in the film The Martian.

fun_fact: T.E. Lawrence described Wadi Rum as 'vast, echoing, and God-like' in his memoir Seven Pillars of Wisdom.

riddle_text: The most remote inhabited place on Earth has no airport. To reach its 250 souls, you sail six days from the nearest land. Their surnames number only eight — everyone is related. A volcano erupted in 1961 and the entire population was evacuated to England. They returned two years later because they missed home. Home is here, in the middle of absolutely nothing.

clues.text: This island is the most remote permanently inhabited archipelago in the world. The nearest inhabited island, Saint Helena, is 2,437 km away. There is no airstrip.
Its only settlement is Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, population approximately 250. All residents share one of eight surnames due to centuries of isolation.
It is a British Overseas Territory located in the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly equidistant between South Africa and South America.
This British territory in the South Atlantic is the most remote inhabited island on Earth, reachable only by a six-day boat journey.

fun_fact: When the islanders were evacuated to England in 1961, they hated it so much they all returned as soon as the volcano cooled down.

riddle_text: Where the cold is so absolute that eyelashes freeze and cars must never be switched off. At minus 71.2 degrees, a breath becomes a cloud before it forms. The river nearby does not freeze — it is too fast. Cattle still live here because they must. Children still go to school until the temperature drops below minus 52. This is the coldest permanently inhabited settlement humanity has ever managed.

clues.text: This village recorded the lowest temperature ever measured for a permanently inhabited place: −71.2°C (−96.2°F) on 26 January 1926. The name means 'non-freezing water' in Yakut.
Located in the Sakha Republic (Yakutia), it has approximately 500 inhabitants. Burying the dead requires a blowtorch to thaw the permafrost first.
Situated in the Siberian region of the world's largest country by land area, roughly 350km south of the Arctic Circle on the Indigirka River.
This tiny village in Siberia, Russia, holds the verified record for the coldest inhabited place ever recorded on Earth.

fun_fact: At −50°C in Oymyakon, boiling water thrown into the air freezes before it hits the ground.

riddle_text: A concrete island shaped like a battleship floats in a Japanese sea — an entire city abandoned overnight. Miners once packed its brutalist towers at the highest population density ever recorded on Earth. When the coal ran out, they left in 1974. Jungle has no foothold here — only concrete crumbling to the sea. A Bond villain found it fitting for his lair.

clues.text: Known as Battleship Island (Gunkanjima in Japanese), this former coal mining facility was once the most densely populated place on Earth at 835 people per hectare.
It was abandoned in 1974 when Mitsubishi closed its coal operations. It was used as the villain's island lair in the James Bond film Skyfall (2012).
Located approximately 15km off the coast of Nagasaki in Kyushu — the southwestern island of an East Asian archipelago nation.
This abandoned Japanese island near Nagasaki, nicknamed Battleship Island, was the setting for the villain's lair in Skyfall.

fun_fact: At its peak in 1959, Hashima Island housed 5,259 people in an area of just 6.3 hectares — denser than present-day Manhattan times ten.

riddle_text: Acid pools of electric yellow and chartreuse bubble beside pillars of crystallised salt in colours that seem to belong to another solar system. The average annual temperature here is the highest recorded for any inhabited location on Earth. The ground itself is below sea level — a geological depression being pulled apart by three tectonic plates simultaneously. Beauty and hostility share every inch.

clues.text: This hydrothermal field holds the world's highest average annual temperature at 34.4°C (93.9°F) and sits 130 metres below sea level in one of Earth's most geologically active zones.
Its luminous acid pools, salt pillars, and gas vents are created by the intersection of three tectonic plates — the Nubian, Somali, and Arabian — at the Danakil Depression.
Located in the Afar Region of a northeast African country known as the origin of Arabica coffee and home to the ancient rock-hewn churches of Lalibela.
This extraordinary hydrothermal field in the Danakil Depression, Ethiopia, is considered one of the most hostile environments on Earth.

fun_fact: The pools at Dallol have a pH close to zero — among the most acidic naturally occurring water on Earth — yet microbial life has been found surviving there.

riddle_text: At the end of the world, where the Southern Ocean rages without interruption around the entire globe, a jagged archipelago rises from the fury. It has no permanent civilian population. No flights exist. A French research station of 45–100 scientists is all that proves humanity has noticed. The wind here is not a feature of the weather — it is the weather itself. Rabbits introduced by whalers have stripped it nearly bare.

clues.text: This sub-Antarctic archipelago was discovered by French navigator Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen-Trémarec in 1772. It consists of one large island and approximately 300 smaller ones, covering 7,215 km².
Its only human presence is the Port-aux-Français research station. It is sometimes called the Desolation Islands. Wild rabbits introduced in the 19th century have devastated its native vegetation.
Located in the southern Indian Ocean at approximately 49°S, it is a French territory roughly equidistant from South Africa, Australia, and Antarctica.
These remote French islands in the southern Indian Ocean, nicknamed the Desolation Islands, have no airport and no permanent civilian population.

fun_fact: The Kerguelen Islands' isolation is so extreme that the island's indigenous Kerguelen cabbage was historically the only fresh food available to prevent scurvy for passing sailors.
